summary: Walkback is an interactive Marswalk planning simulator for Gale Boxwork, Jezero Delta Front, and Jezero Western Rim. It combines orbital elevation and imagery, regional geology, and observations from Curiosity and Perseverance to help a crew choose science stops and plan a return to a simulated habitat. The planner estimates outbound and return times from the terrain, compares science itineraries against time, battery, oxygen, and daylight limits, and lets crews explore what happens when a path is blocked, suit battery drops, or a rover breaks down.
details:
The Three Chosen Landscapes:

The experience begins on an interactive Mars globe and opens into Gale Crater's boxwork, Jezero's delta front, or Jezero's western rim. Each location combines orbital imagery and elevation with localized rover observations and curated science destinations.

Users can switch on reachability, steep-ground, boulder, contour, shaded-relief, relative nighttime-infrared, rover-path, and target layers. Jezero also includes mapped geologic units. These layers help explain why a destination is interesting and why the route to it may be difficult.

Plan the science or choose your own route

In Science mission mode, users select a scientific goal and number of stops. Walkback chooses a compatible itinerary, accounts for time spent working, and checks the round trip against the selected limits. Goals include investigating Gale's boxwork ridges and hollows, exploring evidence of ancient water at Jezero, and comparing crater-rim geology. Users can inspect proposed stops and consider alternatives.

In Manual route mode, users choose stops directly on the map, change their order, and adjust work time. Both modes let users choose one or two astronauts, travel on foot or by rover, set departure time, and adjust walking speed, slope limits, suit supplies, reserves, and the mission time margin. Fastest and gentlest route options let users explore different terrain and time tradeoffs; changing the route preference can also change which science stops are feasible


Understand the return before committing

The mission timeline shows the visiting order, arrival and work periods, and return time. The route summary and terrain profile show duration, distance, elevation, steep ground, the longest return, and suit supplies remaining.

Walkback explains its Go, Caution, and No-go results through individual checks. For two astronauts, each suit is considered independently, so the crew's battery and oxygen limits can be set by different people. Supplies below the chosen reserve can make a plan infeasible even when the displayed balance is still above zero. Incomplete obstacle coverage is reported as uncertainty.

Rover missions include a walkback check: could the crew return on foot if the vehicle failed? Where supported, the planner also combines driving with parking and walking to a target.

Ask what happens when the plan changes

Users can simulate reduced battery, reduced oxygen, a blocked path, a solar event, or a rover breakdown. Walking-mission replanning tests which remaining science stops still fit and offers return alternatives: the fastest way home, a route that minimizes the steepest slope encountered, or retracing the path already walked. A rover breakdown evaluates the walking return from the selected failure point. The solar-event scenario estimates how much of that return overlaps a modeled historical radiation event.

How it works & The Math Behind it:

Computing the return and choosing science stops

Dijkstra’s algorithm computes the fastest modeled time from the habitat to each terrain cell and back. We run the search in both directions because uphill and downhill travel have different costs. A cell is reachable for one science stop when the outbound trip, work, and return fit within the usable EVA time.For a fixed set of walking stops, Held–Karp dynamic programming finds the fastest visiting order. When Walkback selects the stops, it evaluates ordered itineraries of up to six targets and ranks feasible plans by science relevance, mapped-unit diversity, and elapsed time.

Curiosity’s documented drilling locations support questions about Gale’s boxwork ridges and hollows. At Jezero, the planner can select stops in distinct geologic units to compare evidence of past water activity. We apply a 200 m buffer around interpreted contacts before counting a stop toward geologic diversity. Approximate rover waypoint pins for samples also do not count as confident unit assignments. Curiosity drilling record · USGS Jezero geology

Turning Mars terrain into travel time

We build the route grid from orbital elevations. On the Western Rim, we blend the HiRISE terrain model prepared for Mars 2020 with the 20 m CTX model. The planning grid has 3.125 m spacing, with underlying terrain detail varying by source coverage. Mars 2020 HiRISE terrain model · Jezero CTX elevation model

Horn’s 3×3 gradient estimates a cell’s steepest terrain slope from the surrounding elevations. Each step also has a signed grade based on its elevation change Δz and horizontal distance 𝑑.

These two slope checks account for climbing, descending, and traversing across a steep hillside. We chose an adjustable 20° default based on a NASA xEVA suit design assumption used in Artemis surface planning. Horn’s terrain-gradient method · NASA Artemis EVA capability study

We rescale Tobler’s hiking function to the crew’s chosen flat-ground speed 𝑣0 in km/h. Step time is the three-dimensional step length divided by walking speed, multiplied by 𝑚v = 1.25 when entering rocky ground.

The rocky-ground multiplier is our planning assumption. Apollo drive reports informed the rover’s 8 km/h flat-speed parameter and our approximation of a 2.5% reduction in flat speed per degree of slope. Tobler’s hiking function · NASA Apollo rover drive reports

Turning orbital shadows into obstacles

We adapted a method used in Mars landing-site research to estimate boulder sizes from shadows. The detector compares each pixel with its local background and estimates the Sun direction from the alignment of shadows and bright faces. It measures the shadow’s width across that direction. The factor 0.25 comes from the HiRISE imagery’s 25 cm pixel scale.

Under our routing rules, detections at least 1.5 m wide block walking cells. Detections from 1.0 m to under 1.5 m slow walking. Both classes block rover travel. Each logged detection includes an estimated size, source image tile, and confidence level. Published HiRISE shadow-based rock detection

Checking suit reserves and daylight

NASA’s Extravehicular Mobility Unit documentation provides the reference values for our suit model: 26.6 Ah of battery capacity, a 3.8 A reference load, and a seven-hour oxygen budget. We assume 18.5 V to convert battery capacity and current to watt-hours and watts. For travel and work times in seconds, Walkback computes

Here 𝑃 is power in watts and 𝑟 is the oxygen consumption rate in oxygen-minutes per elapsed minute. With two astronauts, the lower battery reading and lower oxygen reading govern their respective reserve checks. NASA EMU battery report · NASA EVA hardware overview

We use NASA GISS Mars24 for seasonal solar declination δ and the Martian sol length of 88,775.244 seconds. With site latitude ϕ and local solar hour angle 𝐻, we calculate solar elevation α.
The flat-horizon crossings estimate sunrise and sunset. We divide elapsed seconds by one twenty-fourth of a sol to compare the planned return time with local sunset. NASA GISS Mars24 equations

Replanning when conditions change

After a simulated battery loss or path blockage, Walkback starts from the crew’s current position and tests which remaining science stops still fit. The crew can compare the fastest path home, a minimax path that minimizes the steepest slope encountered, and a retrace of the route already walked.

In rover mode, we apply Apollo’s walkback principle by checking whether the crew could return on foot from points along the proposed drive with the supplies remaining. If a target lies beyond drivable terrain, the planner finds reachable parking and adds the walking trip to the itinerary. NASA surface rover walkback technical brief

Solar-event exposure

Curiosity’s Radiation Assessment Detector measured excess absorbed dose of 1,730.55 µGy during the 20 May 2024 event at Gale Crater. The event lasted 41 hours 55 minutes, peaked 53 minutes after local detection, and reached 10% of its cumulative dose by minute 57. We use those measurements to fit a dose-rate curve with a linear rise and exponential decline. Walkback integrates the fitted rate over the part of the crew’s return that overlaps the event.



Published Curiosity RAD event analysis

Benefits and intended impact

Walkback helps users decide which science is worth the time and resources it takes to reach, study, and return from a site. A mission-planning team can compare priorities and contingency routes. Students and educators can explore those same decisions using observations from real Mars missions. Our goal is to make the return trip an explicit part of choosing where to do science.

Tools and development

We built the browser application with TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, and Canvas 2D. Web Workers run terrain processing and route searches off the interface thread.

We used Python, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio/GDAL, PyProj, Shapely, Fiona, and Pillow to prepare the map data, and Vitest to test the planner. The prototype runs on a standard computer in a web browser.

Validation and limits

  • Rover-track cross-check. Our boulder detector marked 3.44% of all Gale map cells as blocked, compared with 1.00% of cells along Curiosity’s localized traverse. This comparison helped us tune detection on Gale’s sharpened orbital imagery.
  • Software verification. The project passed 123 tests, including checks for route continuity, slope limits, resource calculations, and replanning on bundled Mars terrain.
  • Factors affecting the results. We considered terrain resolution, gaps in boulder coverage, uncertain geologic contacts, and the limits of transferring terrestrial walking and lunar rover models to Mars. Habitat locations, work durations, and failures are simulated. Walkback reports whether a route is feasible under those assumptions and the selected crew settings.
